title: Environmental economics

definition.text: The branch of economics that studies environmental problems and the economic effects of policies meant to deal with them.

facts.text: It weighs the costs and benefits of different policies on air pollution, water quality, toxic substances, solid waste and global warming.
Market failure, where markets do not put resources to their best use, is the idea at its centre.
Most environmental economists are trained as economists and use economic tools on problems where the market's 'invisible hand' cannot be relied on.
Putting an economic value on the environment is a major topic, because many natural resources carry no market price at all.
The name became popular in the 1960s, but links between economics and the environment go back to Condorcet, Adam Smith, Malthus and Ricardo.
Ronald Coase's economic solution to environmental problems is credited with settling it as a sub-field of economics.
It was once separate from natural resource economics, but the two are now hard to tell apart.
Its main professional bodies are the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists and the European Association for Environmental and Resource Economists.

notes: S:60b7b6319f6a says the field grew popular 'in the 19th century' in a section headed 20th Century; probably a slip for the 20th century.

definition.text: A cost or benefit that falls on a third party who had no part in the activity that caused it.

facts.text: Externalities are parts of production or consumption that carry no price.
Air pollution from cars is one: neither car makers nor drivers pay its cost to society.
Pollution of the environment is the textbook example of a negative externality.
Because the market price does not reflect the true cost or benefit to society, resources could be better allocated, so externalities are a kind of market failure.
Alfred Marshall first developed the idea in the 1890s, and Arthur Pigou brought it wider attention in the 1920s.
Governments often try to 'internalize' externalities so that prices include all the costs and benefits, most often by taxing whoever causes them.
Setting the right tax is hard because regulators rarely have full information about the externality.
The idea is now used beyond economics, in environmental science, public health and urban planning.

definition.text: A harmful side effect of producing or consuming something that lands on an unrelated third party and is not counted in the market price.

facts.text: It is also called an external cost or external diseconomy, and can arise in either production or consumption.
Formally, it is the gap between what an action costs the person taking it and what it costs society.
Air pollution from burning fossil fuels damages crops, materials, historic buildings and public health.
A neighbour's loud late-night music causing lost sleep is a consumption example.
Because they are Pareto inefficient, negative externalities are treated as more of a problem than positive ones.

definition.text: A beneficial side effect of an activity that helps an unrelated third party, without that party paying for it.

facts.text: It is also called an external benefit or external economy, and like a negative one can come from production or consumption.
A beekeeper's bees pollinate the crops around them as a side effect of honey production.
Planting trees makes nearby properties look nicer and cleans the surrounding area.
Even positive externalities are a market failure, because the good ends up produced below the best amount.
They invite free riding: a neighbour enjoying the bees for free has no reason to buy bees himself.

definition.text: A side effect in which one person's purchase of a status good lowers the value others get from similar goods they already own.

facts.text: It grows from the ideas of conspicuous consumption, buying to show off status, and positional goods, whose value depends on comparison with what others own.
When one member of a group buys a luxury car, others may feel they must upgrade too, wasting resources and widening inequality.
It can trigger a cascade of overconsumption as people spend to keep their relative standing.

definition.text: An externality that does not affect the marginal consumer, so it causes no market inefficiency.

facts.text: James Buchanan and Craig Stubblebine introduced the idea in 1962.
Because it acts only away from where the market clears, it does not misallocate resources and needs no policy action.

title: Causes of externalities

definition.text: The view that externalities come mainly from poorly defined property rights and from the costs of making trades.

facts.text: Land and money are easy to own, but air, water and wild animals cross borders freely, so people use them without paying the full cost.
A person who gets a flu shot cannot own a share of the herd immunity it creates, so may skip it.
Transaction costs, the costs of making a trade, block some worthwhile exchanges; without them people could bargain away every externality.

contested_note: The source page itself tags this section as one-sided, calling its property-rights account a narrow libertarian reading of Coase.

definition.text: A standard supply and demand graph with an extra curve added to show how an externality pushes the market away from the best quantity for society.

facts.text: For pollution, the private cost of making a good sits below its social cost by the amount of the external cost.
Buyers counting only private cost end up at a lower price and higher quantity than the efficient one.
Efficiency requires producing only while the marginal social benefit exceeds the marginal social cost.
In the steel example, people buy and use too much steel, and society would be better off if the extra units were never made.
With an external benefit such as vaccination, the private benefit falls short of the social benefit.
The gap is not fixed by competitive markets; some collective answer is needed, such as courts, bans or green taxes.

title: Ecological critique of externalities

definition.text: The argument from ecological and heterodox economists that treating environmental harm as an occasional 'externality' misreads how the economy works.

facts.text: Karl William Kapp called the term a misnomer, arguing that businesses shift costs onto others as a normal way of making profit.
Clive Spash argues that fixing the odd externality leaves the deeper, system-wide problem untouched.
Future generations, not yet born, cannot influence today's prices at all.
Heterodox economists instead argue for a theory of social costs that prevents harm through the precautionary principle.

contested_note: Ecological economists dispute the mainstream view that internalizing externalities can correct environmental harm.

title: Environmental versus ecological economics

definition.text: The contrast between environmental economics, which applies standard economics to the environment, and ecological economics, which treats the economy as a part of the ecosystem.

facts.text: Ecological economists stress 'strong' sustainability and reject the idea that human-made capital can stand in for natural capital.
Most environmental economists trained as economists, while most ecological economists trained as ecologists.
Ecological economics is described as more pluralistic and more focused on long-term sustainability and scale.
Environmental economics is seen as idealistic about the price system, ecological economics as more realistic about factors outside it.

contested_note: The two schools hold conflicting views traced to different philosophical foundations.

definition.text: Putting an economic value on the environment and natural resources, many of which have no market price.

facts.text: When natural assets go unpriced, they tend to be both overused and underinvested in.
Non-use values include existence value, option value and bequest value, such as wanting to leave a pristine environment to one's children.
Use values can be read from behaviour, such as the cost of recreational trips or house prices in hedonic methods.
Non-use values are usually estimated with surveys such as contingent valuation or choice modelling.
Contingent valuation asks people what they would pay for an environmental good, or accept for its loss.

definition.text: Government payments that reward companies more for exploiting natural resources than for protecting them.

facts.text: The damage these subsidies do to nature has been conservatively estimated at $4-$6 trillion U.S. dollars per year.
The largest support the fossil fuel, agriculture and water sectors.

definition.text: The choice between fixing pollution with direct rules on polluters and fixing it with prices, taxes or tradeable permits.

facts.text: Command-and-control rules often set the same emission limit for every firm, even though some can cut pollution cheaply and others only at high cost.
Economic instruments find the cheapest cuts first: under permit trading a firm abates only if that costs less than paying another firm to do it.
A pollution tax gives a 'dynamic incentive' that keeps working even as pollution falls.
The two are less different than often claimed: fines act like a tax, and both need monitoring and enforcement.
Permit trading has had some success in practice, such as the US sulphur dioxide program and the EU Emissions Trading Scheme.

definition.text: The value of nature that industries use up without paying for it, which would change their profits if it were priced.

facts.text: The world's largest industries burn about $7.3 trillion of free natural capital per year.
Those industries would hardly be profitable if they had to pay for this damage.
Cattle ranching and farming in South America ranks second, with a natural capital cost of 312.1 billion dollars against revenue of 16.6 billion.
